title: Participles in Phrases
short: Participles agree with the noun they describe, take objects, and can stand alone as nouns: sḏmw "those who hear".
trouble: Students forget agreement: a participle describing a woman takes -t.

blocks.html: Participles behave like adjectives (Active Participles), so they agree with the noun they describe, and like adjectives they can also stand alone as nouns.

A participle takes the ending of its noun: no ending for a masculine singular (z sḏm "a man who hears"), -t for a feminine (zꜣt sḏmt "a daughter who hears"), -w for a plural (nṯrw sḏmw "gods who hear"). Standing alone it is a noun: sḏmw "those who hear", sḏmt "she who hears".

This is the agreement you already know from adjectives: zꜣt nfrt "a good daughter". A participle is a verbal adjective, so it follows the same rule. Adjectives can stand for a person ("the good", "the great"), and so can participles; the ending then shows who is meant, one man, one woman, or several.

blocks.title: Make it agree
blocks.q: Write "the goddess who knows the name" with nṯrt, rḫ and rn.

blocks.title: Alone, as a noun
steps: No noun stands before ḏdw, so it is a noun itself.
The -w makes it plural: "those who speak".

blocks.html: The feminine form alone often means "that which, what", a neuter: ḏdt "what is said", jrt "what is done" (with a passive sense). Egyptian has no separate neuter, and the feminine fills that role, as it does in ḫt nbt "everything".

blocks.title: A feminine participle
blocks.q: Write "the daughter who speaks the truth" with zꜣt, ḏd and mꜣꜥt.
steps: zꜣt is feminine, so the participle takes -t: ḏdt.

blocks.html: In writing, the endings are not always shown, especially the -w of the plural, which may be replaced by the three plural strokes or left out. Transliterations usually restore the ending that grammar requires, so when you write a phrase in transliteration, add the ending even if the hieroglyphs skip it.

Forgetting agreement. A participle describing a woman takes -t, even if the verb's object is masculine: zꜣt sḏmt ḫrw, not zꜣt sḏm ḫrw. Check: the participle agrees with the noun before it, never with its own object.
